1#main: The laws of kilay zera'im and its details. In it are 40 seifim. One who sows two species of seeds together in Eretz Yisrael receives lashes, as it says, "your field you shall not sow kilayim"—whether one sows or weeds or covers, such as when there was one wheat and one barley or one bean and one lentil placed on the ground and he covered them with earth, whether with his hand or with his foot—he receives lashes. And whether one sows in the ground or in a perforated pot; but one who sows in an unperforated pot receives lashes of rebellion.
2#main: It is forbidden to sow kilayim for a non-Jew; and it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to sow kilay zera'im for him. And it is forbidden to maintain them in his field except that he uproots them; and if he maintained them he does not receive lashes. And it is permitted for an Israelite to sow kilay zera'im with his hand in the Diaspora, and even to mix seeds initially and sow them in the Diaspora—it is permitted. And these matters are words of tradition.
3#main: It is forbidden only because of kilay zera'im for seeds fit for human food; but bitter herbs and the like from roots not fit except for medicine and the like have no kilay zera'im. Seeds are divided into three parts: one called grain—the five species of grain; the second called legumes, such as beans, peas, lentils, rice, millet, sesame, poppy, and sparrow (meaning: like a pomegranate full of seeds—pashor in vernacular; and sparrow is a legume species—tsitsirik in vernacular), and the like; the third called garden seeds—the rest of seeds not fit for human food but whose fruit of that seed is human food, such as onion seed, garlic seed, grass seed, turnip seed, and the like; and flax seed is in the category of garden seeds.
4#main: When all these seed types are sown and grow, the plant is called grass all the time the seed is not recognizable; and it is called vegetable. And among garden seeds there are those customarily sown as fields, such as flax and mustard—these are called seed species; and among garden seeds there are those people do not customarily sow as fields but only small beds, such as turnip, cucumber, beets, onions, coriander (meaning: like large seed—Targum kisbara; coriander white—koliandro in vernacular), cress, bitter herbs, and the like—these are called vegetable species.
5#main: Seed in which another seed became mixed—if one was one in twenty-four, such as a se'ah of wheat mixed in twenty-four se'ah of barley, behold it is forbidden to sow the mixture until he diminishes the wheat or adds to the barley. And if he sowed, he receives lashes. And whatever is kilayim with the seed combines to one in twenty-four. How so? Twenty-four se'ah of wheat in which two kav of barley, two kav of lentils, and two kav of beans became mixed—behold he does not sow all until he diminishes a se'ah of the mixture and sorts part of it, or adds to the wheat—for barley, lentils, and beans are all kilayim with wheat.
6#main: In what case is this said? When grain species became mixed one with another, or legume species one with another, or grain became mixed with legumes or legumes with grain. But garden seed mixed with grain or legumes—their measure is one in twenty-four of what is sown per se'ah of that species: if mixed in a se'ah of grain or legumes, he does not sow until he diminishes or adds to the grain. How so? Mustard mixed with grain—and behold mustard is sown a kav per se'ah—if one twenty-fourth of the kav mixed in a se'ah of grain or legumes, he must diminish. And likewise if this garden species is sown two se'ah per se'ah and half a kav mixed in every se'ah of grain or legumes, he diminishes. Therefore grain in which flax seed mixed—if there were three quarters in every se'ah, behold he diminishes; and if not, he need not diminish, for per se'ah they sow three se'ah of flax seed. And on this manner we estimate all other seeds.
7#main: In what case is this said? When he did not intend to mix and did not intend to sow the two species that became mixed. But if he intended to mix seed with another seed, or to sow the two species—even if there was one wheat in a large pile of barley, it is forbidden to sow it, and likewise all similar cases.
8#main: One who sows one species and when it grew he saw kilayim in it—if the other species was one in twenty-four in the field, behold he harvests until he diminishes it, because of marit ayin lest they say he sowed kilayim intentionally—whether the other species that grew was grain and legumes in grain, or garden seed in grain and legumes and in garden seed. And if what grew was less than this, he need not diminish it.
9#main: In what case is this said? When there is place for suspicion; but when the matters indicate this is not from the field owner's knowledge but grew on their own, we do not obligate him to diminish. How so? Such as grain in which darnel and clover grew—and their seed is for human food—and species of grasses grew in it that this one ruins, and all similar cases. And how does one know clover was sown for human food? When it was sown in beds and has a border around it. And likewise a threshing floor place in which many species grew—we do not obligate to uproot, for it is known he does not want plants to grow in the threshing floor place; and if he removed part of them, we tell him uproot all except one species, for he revealed his intent that he wants the rest to remain.
10#main: One does not plant vegetables inside a stump of sycamore (meaning: a tree trunk cut and its roots remain in the ground—and sycamore is a fig species of the forest) and the like.
11#main: One who buries bundles of turnip, cucumber, and the like under a tree—even under a vine—if part of the leaves were exposed, he is not concerned, for he does not want their rooting; and if they are not a bundle, or the leaves were not exposed, he is concerned because of kilayim.
12#main: A field that was sown and he harvested the seed and roots remained in the ground—even though they do not produce a plant except after many years—another species may not be sown in that field until he uproots the roots.
13#main: His field was sown with wheat and he reconsidered to sow it barley—before the wheat sprouts he waits for it until the wheat spoils and rots in the ground, about three days if his field was moist; and afterward he turns them with a plowshare and sows the other species. And he need not turn all of it until no wheat remains unuprooted, but he plows the field as they plow it before rain so it will be moist. If wheat grew and afterward he reconsidered to sow it barley—he turns over and afterward sows them. And if he brought his animal into it and it cropped the plant, behold it is permitted to sow another species.
14#main: There are among seeds species that will be one species for many forms because of variation of places and the work farmers do until they appear like two species; and even though they do not resemble one another, since they are one species they are not kilayim one with another. And there are among seeds two species that resemble one another and their form is close to being one form, and nevertheless since they are two species, behold these are forbidden one with another. How so? Garden cress with field cress, field endives with field endives, field leeks with field leeks, mountain coriander with coriander, mustard with Egyptian mustard, Egyptian gourd with pickled gourd (meaning: a bitter gourd species sweetened with hot ash)—they are not kilayim one with another. And likewise wheat with darnel, barley with wild barley, spelt with shifin, beans with sparrow, vetch with topach (meaning: vetch and topach are fine seed species—shaua in Arabic; and cucumber—Jerusalem Talmud: fruit coming from watermelon; kishut or from watermelon and topach; and some say it is the fruit called citron in vernacular; trubador is a cabbage species with small heads; beets are a vegetable species—boliti in vernacular; leeks are a beet species; nefusim are a cucumber species; laptan—Aruch: maroy in vernacular) and white beans with shaua, kishut with cucumber, cabbage with trubador, beets with leeks—they are not kilayim one with another. But cucumber with nefusim, mustard with laptan, Greek gourd with Egyptian gourd or with pickled gourd—even though they resemble one another, behold these are kilayim one with another. And likewise in a tree when there are two species resembling one another in leaves or in fruits—since they are two species, behold they are kilayim as explained in siman 295.
15#main: There are other seeds and trees that even though they are two species by nature, since the leaves of this resemble the leaves of that, or the fruit of this resembles the fruit of that—a great resemblance until they appear like two shades of one species—they were not concerned for kilayim one with another. How so? Turnip with cucumber—they are not kilayim because their fruits are equal; turnip with nefus—they are not kilayim because the leaves are equal; but cucumber with nefus—even though the leaves resemble one another and fruit resembles fruit, behold these are kilayim because the taste of this fruit is very far from the taste of that fruit; and likewise all similar cases.
16#main: How much does one distance between two seed species that are kilayim one with another so they are separated one from another? But if they appear sown mixed, behold it is forbidden. And there are many measures in this distancing—all according to the size of the field sown and according to the abundance of leaves and the spread of suckers. How so? His field was sown with one grain species and he seeks to sow beside it in another field another grain species—he distances between them a beit rova, which is about ten amot and a fifth of an amah on ten amot and a fifth of an amah, square, whether from the middle or from the side. And if between them there was not this measure, it is forbidden and he does not receive lashes until they are close within six handbreadths.
17#main: His field was sown with vegetable and he seeks to sow beside it another vegetable field—even gourd—he distances between the two fields six handbreadths on sixteen, square, whether from the side or from the middle; and less than this measure is forbidden, and he does not receive lashes until they are close within a handbreadth.
18#main: If one of the two fields was sown with grain and the second beside it with vegetable—or gourd—he distances between them a beit rova.
19#main: In what case is this said? When he must distance these measures between two fields. But if his field was sown with vegetable and he wishes to sow beside it a row of vegetable of another species, it suffices to make between the field and the row one furrow a handbreadth long and six handbreadths only, and its width like its depth.
20#main: His field was sown with grain and he wishes to sow within it a row of vegetable—even a row of gourds whose leaves are long and intertwine—he distances between them six handbreadths. And if gourd leaves spread and entered the grain and intertwined with it, he uproots from the grain before the gourd until the leaves do not mix. And all the more so if he sowed a row of one species and a row of another species, it suffices that between them there be one furrow (meaning: the plowshare's groove is called gedudim and the height is called a furrow).
21#main: If he distanced between the two species the appropriate distancing and this species leaned over that species—whether grain leaned on grain, or vegetable on grain, or grain on vegetable—all is permitted, for he distanced according to the measure, except Greek gourd which spreads greatly; therefore if it leaned, he uproots from before it.
22#main: If between the two species there was a pit, or fallow ground, or a stone fence (meaning: a fence of stones arranged one on another without mortar), or a path, or a fence ten handbreadths high, or a ditch ten handbreadths deep and four wide, or a tree providing shade on the ground, or a rock ten high and four wide—behold it is permitted to adjoin one side to these and the other species to the other side, since each of these separates between them—behold they appear separated one from another. In what case is this said? When he needs distancing or a separating matter when he sowed within his field. But if his field was sown with wheat, his friend is permitted to sow barley beside it, as it says "your field you shall not sow kilayim"—the prohibition is only when he sows his field as kilayim, for it does not say "the land shall not be sown kilayim." And not only that, but even if he sowed within his field barley near wheat and barley seed extended until it adjoined his friend's field sown with barley, behold it is permitted, because the barley in his field appears as the end of his friend's field.
23#main: His field was sown with wheat and his friend's field beside it was sown with wheat—it is permitted for him to sow one furrow of flax beside his wheat adjoining his friend's field, for the viewer knows there is no way to sow one furrow of flax; and he did not intend this except to test his field whether it is fit to sow flax—if not, it is as though he sows to ruin it. But another species is forbidden to sow between these two fields that are one species until he distances within his own.
24#main: His field and his friend's field beside him were sown with two grain species—he does not sow between them mustard and charua even one furrow, because people sow from these one furrow alone. But if both fields were sown with two vegetable species, it is permitted to sow between them mustard or charua, for it is permitted to surround mustard around every species except grain, because they do not harm it.
25#main: If the corner of this seed touched the side of the other seed within his field, behold it is permitted because they appear separated one from another; and all the more so if the corner of seed touched the corner of the other seed, because they appear like the end of a field that is permitted without distancing and without separation.
26#main: It is permitted to sow two rows one beside the other of cucumbers, and two rows beside them of gourds, and two rows of Egyptian beans, and a furrow between each species and species. But he does not sow one row of cucumbers and one row of gourds and one row of Egyptian beans, even though a furrow separates between each species and species, because these species have long leaves that spread and intertwine; and if he sowed them row beside row, everything will mix and appear sown mixed.
27#main: His field was sown with one vegetable species and he seeks to sow within it rows of gourds—he uproots from the vegetable the place where he sows a row of gourds and separates between it and the vegetable with a furrow, and leaves from the vegetable a width of twelve amot; and makes a second row of gourds and separates between it and the vegetable with a furrow; and so until where he wishes—so that between every two rows of gourds there are twelve amot. But less than this is forbidden because of leaves intertwining from here and here in the vegetable between them, and everything appears as though sown mixed.
28#main: If a row of gourd was sown—even a single gourd—and he comes to sow grain beside it, he distances a beit rova, for it spread upon it and occupied a large place.
29#main: Everything that is within a beit rova that we distance between two species is counted from the measure, such as a grave and rocks and the like.
30#main: A furrow or water channel that are a handbreadth deep—they sow within them three seed species: one on the lip of the furrow from here, and one from here, and one in the middle.
31#main: It is permitted to plant two species within one hollow—even cucumber and gourd—provided this species leans from above the lip of the hollow to here and the other species leans to the other side and they appear separated one from another. And likewise if he planted four species within the hollow and turned them to its four directions, behold it is permitted.
32#main: One who wishes to sow his field bed by bed (meaning: plots by plots) of each species and species—he distances between each bed and bed two amot by two amot, and narrows and proceeds until between them at the end of the bed there remains only whatever, for behold they appear as though not sown mixed.
33#main: If he wished to make his field bald patches (karachat) of each species and species, he does not make within each se'ah more than nine bald patches—each bald patch a beit rova—and the distance between bald patch and bald patch is close to ten amot less a quarter, for each se'ah is fifty by fifty. And what is the difference between a bed and a bald patch? The bed is long and the bald patch is square.
34#main: Vegetable species that people do not customarily sow except a little—it is permitted to sow from them even five species within one bed that is six by six handbreadths, provided he sows four species on the four directions of the bed and one in the middle, and distances between species and species like a handbreadth and a half so they do not draw nourishment one from another. But more than five species he does not sow even though he distances between them, for many species in such a bed behold are like planted mixed.
35#main: In what case is this said? In a bed that is in a ruin and there is no seed outside it. But a bed among beds—it is forbidden to sow in it five species, for if he sows on every direction of this bed and on every direction of beds surrounding it, everything will appear mixed. And if he bent the leaves in this bed to here and leaves in the bed beside it from here until they appear separated, it is permitted. And likewise if he made a furrow between each bed and bed, it is permitted.
36#main: It is forbidden to sow outside the bed without a furrow and without bending, even opposite the corners of a bed that has no seed—decree lest he sow the four species on the four directions of the bed and sow other species outside opposite the corners, and everything be found mixed.
37#main: If the bed was six by six and had a border a handbreadth high and a handbreadth wide around, it is permitted to sow in it even eighteen species—three on each border and border and six in the middle, and he distances between each species and species a handbreadth and a half. And he does not sow the head of the turnip inside the border lest it fill it more than this. More than this he does not sow. And it is forbidden to sow in a bed seed species in this manner because they appear as kilayim; but vegetable species, since people do not customarily sow them except little by little, behold it is permitted as explained.
38#main: A border that was a handbreadth high and he sowed in it many species as explained, and it diminished from a handbreadth after being sown in it—it is valid, for it was valid from its beginning.
39#main: One who wishes to fill his whole garden with many vegetables and not distance between them—he makes the whole garden square beds even six by six, and makes in each bed five circles—four on its four directions and one in the middle—and sows a species in each circle and sows four other species in the four corners of the bed; nine species are found in each bed and they appear separated one from another. And he loses only what is between the circles alone, which he leaves fallow so the circles appear separated from the corners and separated one from another. And if he wished not to lose anything at all—if the circles were sown two, what is between them he sows mixed; and if they were sown mixed, what is between them he sows two, so they appear separated.
40#main: From all these matters it is explained that when there is between two species the appropriate distancing so they do not draw nourishment one from another, we are not concerned for marit ayin; and when they appear separated one from another, we are not concerned for their drawing nourishment, even though they are one beside the other.
41#main: 297—The laws of crossbreeding and the conduct of kilay beheimah. In it are 16 seifim. (297—1) One who mates a male with a female that is not its species—whether in livestock, whether in wild animals and birds, and even in sea animal species—behold he receives lashes.
42#main: (297—2) He does not receive lashes until he inserts with his hand like a tube in a reed. But if he brought them one upon another alone, or aroused them with voice—they give him lashes of rebellion.
43#main: (297—3) It is permitted to bring two species into one pen; and if he saw them mating one with another, he is not obligated to separate them. {Rama: And in a place where there is reason to fear licentiousness that they will do a prohibition, it is forbidden to bring them in even to a pen (Nimukei Yosef on the chapter HaSho'el).}
44#main: (297—4) It is forbidden for an Israelite to give his animal to a non-Jew for mating. {Rama: And likewise any statement to a non-Jew—even for a negative commandment—is forbidden (there). Unless the non-Jew does it for his own benefit (Hagahot Mordechai on Shabbat).}
45#main: (297—5) One who transgressed and mated his animal as kilayim—behold what is born from them is permitted in benefit; and if it was a pure species with a pure species, it is permitted in eating.
46#main: (297—6) Every two species of livestock or wild animal—even though they resemble one another and grow one with another and conceive one from another—since they are two species, they are forbidden because of kilayim. How so? Wolf with dog, village dog (meaning: a dog raised in villages—it is small and resembles a fox) with fox, goats with gazelles, ibexes with sheep, horse with mule, mule with donkey, donkey with wild ass (meaning: a wild donkey growing in the desert)—kilayim one with another.
47#main: (297—7) A species that has wild and domesticated, such as wild ox with ox, and remakh (meaning: a horse from the sons of the Remachim) with horse—they are permitted one with another. But domestic goose with wild goose are kilayim one with another, because the domestic goose lays its eggs inside and the wild goose lays its eggs outside—from which it is clear they are two species.
48#main: (297—8) The koy is kilayim with wild animal and with livestock, and one does not receive lashes on it because it is a doubt.
49#main: (297—9) Those born from kilayim—if their mothers were one species, it is permitted to mate them one with another; and if their mothers were two species, it is forbidden to mate them one with another, even though their fathers were another species. And it is forbidden to mate this offspring even on its mother's species. How so? A mule whose mother was a donkey—it is permitted to mate it on a mule whose mother was a donkey; and it is forbidden to mate it even on a donkey. But a mule whose mother was a horse—it is forbidden to mate it on a mule whose mother was a donkey, and likewise all similar cases. Therefore one who wishes to mate a mule on a mule or to drive with two mules examines the signs of ears and tail and voice—if they resemble one another, it is known their mothers were one species and they are permitted.
50#main: (297—10) It is forbidden to do work with two species, such as to plow and to pull with a wagon and the like—whether one is impure and one pure, whether both impure, whether both pure; whether livestock with livestock such as pig with sheep, or wild with wild such as ibex with elephant, or wild with livestock such as dog with goat, or deer with pig, and the like.
51#main: (297—11) Whether one plows, sows, pulls them with a wagon or stone as one, or drives them as one—even with voice he receives lashes. {Rama: A non-Jew driving kilayim—it is permitted for an Israelite to greet him or speak with him in a loud voice, for we are not concerned lest the animals go because of his voice—for in all prohibitions an unintended act is permitted if it is not a definite outcome (pesik reisha). But if an Israelite walks on the road with a non-Jew and an Israelite's load is on the non-Jew's wagon that he drives as kilayim, the Israelite may not walk near the wagon, for sometimes the wagon is pressed and he will shout at the animals to go quickly—and this is forbidden because of driving kilayim (Terumat HaDeshen siman 298).} But the one who harnesses is exempt until he pulls or until he drives. {Rama: And some say it is forbidden to drive them or pull them only when tied together (Tur in the name of the Rosh); therefore it is permitted for a rider to pull with a rope a dog beside a horse (there in the name of Avi HaEzri). And some disagree (there in the name of R' Efraim).}
52#main: (297—12) A wagon that they were pulling as kilayim—it is forbidden to sit in it even though he did not drive, because his sitting causes them to pull the wagon. And likewise it is forbidden for one to sit in the wagon and one to drive.
53#main: (297—13) Even a hundred who drove as one receive lashes.
54#main: (297—14) If he tied two horses to one wagon, it is forbidden to tie a donkey with them even though the two horses can pull it without the donkey.
55#main: (297—15) A wagon pulling with a wagon of one species—he does not tie one species with a rope neither at the side of the wagon nor behind the wagon. {Rama: Because it pushes the wagon in its walking (Tur).}
56#main: (297—16) It is permitted to do work with a person and livestock or wild animal as one, such as a person plowing with an ox, or pulling a wagon with a donkey, and the like.
